Under [Warren Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Hastings "Warren Hastings"), the consolidation of British imperial rule over Bengal was solidified, with the conversion of a trade area into an occupied territory under a military-civil government, while the formation of a regularised system of legislation was brought in under [John Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Shore,_1st_Baron_Teignmouth "John Shore, 1st Baron Teignmouth"). Acting through [Lord Cornwallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Cornwallis "Lord Cornwallis"), then governor-general, he ascertained and defined the rights of the landholders over the soil. These landholders under the previous system had started, for the most part, as collectors of the revenues, and gradually acquired certain prescriptive rights as quasi-proprietors of the estates entrusted to them by the government. In 1793 Lord Cornwallis declared their rights perpetual, and gave over the land of Bengal to the previous quasi-proprietors or _zamindars_, on condition of the payment of a fixed land tax. This piece of legislation is known as the [Permanent Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_Settlement "Permanent Settlement") of the Land Revenue. It was designed to "introduce" ideas of property rights to India, and stimulate a market in land. The former aim misunderstood the nature of landholding in India, and the latter was an abject failure.

The _Cornwallis Code_, while defining the rights of the proprietors, failed to give adequate recognition to the rights of the under-tenants and the cultivators. This remained a serious problem for the duration of British Rule, as throughout the Bengal Presidency _ryots_ (peasants) found themselves oppressed by rack-renting landlords, who knew that every rupee they could squeeze from their tenants over and above the fixed revenue demanded from the government represented pure profit. Furthermore, the Permanent Settlement took no account of inflation, meaning that the value of the revenue to government declined year by year, whilst the heavy burden on the peasantry grew no less. This was compounded in the early 19th century by compulsory schemes for the cultivation of [opium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium "Opium") and [indigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo "Indigo"), the former by the state, and the latter by British planters. Peasants were forced to grow a certain area of these crops, which were then purchased at below market rates for export. This added greatly to rural poverty.

### Government of India Acts of 1833 and 1853

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bengal_Presidency&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Government of India Acts of 1833 and 1853")]

In 1833, the British Parliament enacted the [Government of India Act 1833](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India_Act_1833 "Government of India Act 1833") abolishing the monopoly rights of the Company and converting it into a purely governing body holding its territories in India in trust of the Crown. The Act relieved the governor-in-councils of Bombay and Madras of their legislative duties and consolidated all legislative functions to the governor-general-in-council of India at Calcutta and created a supreme government of India at Calcutta with the office of governor-general of India replacing the governor-general of Fort William. The act also created for the establishment of a new [Presidency of Agra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Agra "Presidency of Agra") with its own Governor-in-council from the ceded and conquered territories of the Presidency of Fort William and also sought to separate the functions of the Presidency of Fort William from the government of India and governor-general of India in council. This was however never fully implemented and instead another act of Parliament[_[which?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Avoid\_weasel\_words "Wikipedia:Avoid weasel words")_] in 1835 created the [North-Western Provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North-Western_Provinces "North-Western Provinces") with a lieutenant-governor at Agra and also provided for the creation of a similar arrangement with a lieutenant-governor of Bengal. All four provinces, i.e., North-Western Provinces, Bengal Presidency, Madras Presidency and Bombay Presidency were equal in status and independent of each other, subordinate only to the government of India.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-30) New conquests in Punjab (1849), Burma (1826) and Oudh (1856) were constituted as Chief Commissioner's Provinces directly administered by the government of India. The [Government of India Act 1853](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India_Act_1853?action=edit&redlink=1 "Government of India Act 1853 (page does not exist)") finally allocated a lieutenant-governor to Bengal, which until now had been administered by the governor-general of India. The act also allocated lieutenant-governors to Punjab and Burma. The [Bengal Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Army "Bengal Army") and the Bengal Civil Service continued to operate in the three lieutenant governorships, however they were under the control of the government of India rather than the Bengal government. The Bengal Civil Service was merged into the Indian Civil Service later along with the other two civil services and the Bengal Army was finally amalgamated into the new [Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Army "British Indian Army") in 1904–5, after a lengthy struggle over its reform between [Lord Kitchener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Kitchener,_1st_Earl_Kitchener "Herbert Kitchener, 1st Earl Kitchener"), the commander-in-chief, and [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon"), the Viceroy.

### Straits Settlements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bengal_Presidency&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Straits Settlements")]

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Photographic_Views_of_Singapore_Plate_01_Johnston%27s_Pier.jpg/250px-Photographic_Views_of_Singapore_Plate_01_Johnston%27s_Pier.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photographic_Views_of_Singapore_Plate_01_Johnston's_Pier.jpg)

Johnston's Pier, Singapore, c.1900

In 1830, the British Straits Settlements on the coast of the [Malacca Straits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malacca_Straits "Malacca Straits") was made a residency of the Presidency of Bengal in Calcutta. The area included the erstwhile [Prince of Wales Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penang_Island "Penang Island") and [Province Wellesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seberang_Perai "Seberang Perai"), as well as the ports of [Malacca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malacca "Malacca") and Singapore.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-autogenerated2-14)

Under the administration of the East India Company, the Settlements were used as [penal settlements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_settlements "Penal settlements") for Indian civilian and military prisoners,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-31) earning them the title of the "Botany Bays of India".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-32):29 The years 1852 and 1853 saw minor uprisings by convicts in Singapore and Penang.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-33):91 Upset with East India Company rule, in 1857 the European population of the Settlements sent a petition to the British Parliament[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-34) asking for direct rule.

### Victorian Era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bengal_Presidency&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Victorian Era")]

In 1859, under the terms of the Queen's Proclamation issued by Queen Victoria, the Bengal Presidency, along with the rest of British India, came under the direct rule of the British Crown.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-victoriap221-35)

The partition of the large province of Bengal, which was decided upon by Lord Curzon, and Cayan Uddin Ahmet, the Chief Secretary of Bengal carried into execution in October 1905. The [Chittagong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong_Division "Chittagong Division"), [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka_Division "Dhaka Division") and [Rajshahi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajshahi_Division "Rajshahi Division") divisions, the [Malda District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malda_District "Malda District") and the States of [Hill Tripura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripura_(princely_state) "Tripura (princely state)"), [Sylhet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylhet "Sylhet") and [Comilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comilla "Comilla") were transferred from Bengal to a new province, [Eastern Bengal and Assam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bengal_and_Assam "Eastern Bengal and Assam"); the five Hindi-speaking states of [Chota Nagpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chota_Nagpur_States "Chota Nagpur States"), namely [Changbhakar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changbhakar_State "Changbhakar State"), [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koriya_State "Koriya State"), [Surguja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surguja_State "Surguja State"), [Udaipur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udaipur_State,_Chhattisgarh "Udaipur State, Chhattisgarh") and [Jashpur State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jashpur_State "Jashpur State"), were transferred from Bengal to the Central Provinces; and [Sambalpur State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sambalpur_State "Sambalpur State") and the five Oriya states of [Bamra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamra_State "Bamra State"), [Rairakhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rairakhol_State "Rairakhol State"), [Sonepur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonepur_State "Sonepur State"), [Patna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patna_State "Patna State") and [Kalahandi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalahandi_State "Kalahandi State") were transferred from the [Central Provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Provinces "Central Provinces") to Bengal.

The [princely states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_states "Princely states") of [Sikkim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikkim "Sikkim") and the [tributary states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tributary_state "Tributary state") of [Odisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odisha "Odisha") and [Chhota Nagpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chhota_Nagpur_States "Chhota Nagpur States") were not part of Bengal, but British relations with them were managed by its government.

The [Indian Councils Act 1909](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Councils_Act_1909 "Indian Councils Act 1909") expanded the legislative councils of Bengal and Eastern Bengal and Assam provinces to include up to 50 nominated and elected members, in addition to three _ex officio_ members from the executive council.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-36)

Bengal's legislative council included 22 nominated members, of which not more than 17 could be officials, and two nominated experts. Of the 26 elected members, one was elected by the [Corporation of Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation_of_Calcutta "Corporation of Calcutta"), six by municipalities, six by district boards, one by the [University of Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Calcutta "University of Calcutta"), five by landholders, four by Muslims, two by the Bengal Chamber of Commerce, and one by the Calcutta Trades Association. Eastern Bengal and Assam's legislative council included 22 nominated members, of which not more than 17 be officials and one representing Indian commerce, and two nominated experts. Of the 18 elected members, three were elected by municipalities, five by district and local boards, two by landowners, four by Muslims, two by the tea interest, one by the jute interest, and one by the Commissioners of the [Port of Chittagong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Chittagong "Port of Chittagong").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-37)

The partition of Bengal proved highly controversial, as it resulted in a largely Hindu West Bengal and a largely Muslim East. Serious popular agitation followed the step, partly on the grounds that this was part of a cynical policy of divide and rule, and partly that the Bengali population, the centre of whose interests and prosperity was Calcutta, would now be divided under two governments, instead of being concentrated and numerically dominant under the one, while the bulk would be in the new division. In 1906–1909 the unrest developed to a considerable extent, requiring special attention from the Indian and Home governments, and this led to the decision being reversed in 1911.

### Reorganisation of Bengal, 1912

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bengal_Presidency&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reorganisation of Bengal, 1912")]

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/King_George_V_1911_color-crop.jpg/250px-King_George_V_1911_color-crop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_George_V_1911_color-crop.jpg)

In 1911, [King-Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_of_India "Emperor of India")[George V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_V "George V") announced the annulment of the first partition of Bengal and the transfer of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj")'s capital from Calcutta to New Delhi

At the [Delhi Durbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Durbar "Delhi Durbar") on 12 December 1911, Emperor George V announced the transfer of the seat of the government of India from Calcutta to Delhi, the reunification of the five predominantly Bengali-speaking divisions into a unified province of Bengal under a governor, the creation of a new province of [Bihar and Orissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar_and_Orissa_Province "Bihar and Orissa Province") under a lieutenant-governor, and that [Assam Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam_Province "Assam Province") would be reconstituted under a chief commissioner. On 21 March 1912 [Thomas Gibson-Carmichael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gibson-Carmichael,_1st_Baron_Carmichael "Thomas Gibson-Carmichael, 1st Baron Carmichael") was appointed governor of Bengal. On 22 March the provinces of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and Assam were constituted.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-38)

The Government of India Act 1919 increased the number of nominated and elected members of the legislative council from 50 to 125, and the franchise was expanded.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency#cite_note-39)[Bihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar_Province "Bihar Province") and [Orissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orissa_Province "Orissa Province") became separate provinces in 1936. Bengal remained in its 1912 boundaries until Independence in 1947, when it was again partitioned between the dominions of India and Pakistan.

The **East India Company** (**EIC**)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-4) was an [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"), and later [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), [joint-stock company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint-stock_company "Joint-stock company") that was founded in 1600 and dissolved in 1874.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Times-5) It was formed for [Indian Ocean trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean_trade "Indian Ocean trade"), initially with the [East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Indies "East Indies") (which included the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") and Southeast Asia), and later with East Asia. The company gained [control of large parts of the Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_rule_in_India "Company rule in India") and [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Hong_Kong "British Hong Kong"). At its peak, the company was the largest corporation in the world by various measures and had its own armed forces in the form of the company's three [presidency armies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_armies "Presidency armies"), totalling about 260,000 soldiers, twice the size of the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") at certain times.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-6)

Originally [chartered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartered_company "Chartered company") as the "Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East-Indies",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-jiscuk-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-8) the company rose to account for half of the world's trade during the mid-1700s and early 1800s,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-onlinegallery-9) particularly in basic commodities including cotton, silk, [indigo dye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo_dye "Indigo dye"), sugar, salt, [spices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice "Spice"), [saltpetre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate "Potassium nitrate"), tea, [gemstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemstone "Gemstone"), and later [opium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium "Opium"). The company also initiated the beginnings of the [British Raj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") in the Indian subcontinent.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-onlinegallery-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-10)

The company eventually came to rule large areas of the Indian subcontinent, exercising [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_armies "Presidency armies") power and assuming administrative functions. Under this government-like rule, the company used torture to extract taxes,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-11) reduced much of the population to poverty[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-12) and enacted policies that resulted in the [Great Bengal famine of 1770](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Bengal_famine_of_1770 "Great Bengal famine of 1770"), during which 10 million people starved to death.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-13)

Company-ruled areas in the region gradually expanded after the [Battle of Plassey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey "Battle of Plassey") in 1757, and by 1858 most of modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, along with [Lower Burma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Burma "Lower Burma"), was either ruled by the company or [princely states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state") closely tied to the company by treaties. Following the [Indian Rebellion of 1857](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857 "Indian Rebellion of 1857"), the [Government of India Act 1858](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India_Act_1858 "Government of India Act 1858") led to the [British Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crown "The Crown") assuming direct control of present-day [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), and [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar") in the form of the new [British Raj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Empire "British Indian Empire").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Conquests-14) The company subsequently experienced recurring problems with its finances, despite frequent government intervention. The company was dissolved in 1874 under the terms of the [East India Stock Dividend Redemption Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Stock_Dividend_Redemption_Act_1873 "East India Stock Dividend Redemption Act 1873") enacted one year earlier, as the Government of India Act had by then rendered it vestigial, powerless, and obsolete. The official government machinery of the British Empire had assumed its governmental functions and absorbed its armies.

In 1577, [Francis Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Drake "Francis Drake") set out on [an expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Drake's_circumnavigation "Francis Drake's circumnavigation") from England to plunder Spanish settlements in South America in search of gold and silver. Sailing in the _[Golden Hind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden\_Hind "Golden Hind"),_ he achieved this, and then sailed across the Pacific Ocean in 1579, known then only to the Spanish and Portuguese. Drake eventually sailed into the [East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Indies "East Indies") and came across the [Moluccas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maluku_Islands "Maluku Islands"), also known as the Spice Islands, and met [Sultan Babullah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babullah_of_Ternate "Babullah of Ternate"). In exchange for linen, gold, and silver, the English obtained a large haul of exotic spices, including cloves and nutmeg. Drake returned to England in 1580 and became a hero; his circumnavigation raised an enormous amount of money for England's coffers, and investors received a return of some 5,000 per cent. Thus started an important element in the eastern design during the late sixteenth century.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Lawson2-15)

With England at war with Spain and Portugal in 1585, trade was now cut off, and Queen [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") resorted to [privateering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privateering "Privateering").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeay19939%E2%80%9311-16) Soon after [Thomas Cavendish's circumnavigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cavendish's_circumnavigation "Thomas Cavendish's circumnavigation") in 1587 and the [Spanish Armada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada "Spanish Armada")'s defeat the following year, the captured Spanish and Portuguese ships and cargoes laid the foundation for further privateering to even more distant zones of the conflict.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMilton199941%E2%80%9342-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-18) London merchants presented a petition to Elizabeth I for permission to sail to the Indian Ocean, and beyond with the Spice Islands of particular interest.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMilton199941%E2%80%9342-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-igi-ii-p454-19) The aim was to deliver a decisive blow to the Spanish and Portuguese monopoly of far-eastern trade.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Wernham-20) Elizabeth granted her permission and in 1591, [James Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lancaster "James Lancaster") in the [_Bonaventure_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_ship_Bonaventure_(1567) "English ship Bonaventure (1567)") with two other ships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Holmes-21) financed by the [Levant Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant_Company "Levant Company"), sailed from England around the [Cape of Good Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_of_Good_Hope "Cape of Good Hope") to the [Arabian Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Sea "Arabian Sea"), becoming the first English expedition to reach India that way.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Holmes-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Anarchy-22):5 Having sailed around [Cape Comorin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Comorin "Cape Comorin") to the [Malay Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_Peninsula "Malay Peninsula"), they preyed on Spanish and Portuguese ships there before returning to England in 1594.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-igi-ii-p454-19)

The biggest prize that galvanised English trade was the seizure of a large Portuguese [carrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrack "Carrack"), the _[Madre de Deus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madre\_de\_Deus "Madre de Deus")_, by [Walter Raleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Raleigh "Walter Raleigh") and the [Earl of Cumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Clifford,_3rd_Earl_of_Cumberland "George Clifford, 3rd Earl of Cumberland") at the [Battle of Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Flores_(1592) "Battle of Flores (1592)") on 13 August 1592.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-McCulloch-23) When she was brought in to [Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth,_Devon "Dartmouth, Devon") she was the largest vessel ever seen in England and she carried chests of jewels, pearls, gold, silver coins, [ambergris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambergris "Ambergris"), cloth, tapestries, pepper, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, [benjamin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzoin_(resin) "Benzoin (resin)") (a highly aromatic balsamic resin used for perfumes and medicines), red dye, [cochineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochineal "Cochineal") and ebony.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-24) Equally valuable was the ship's [rutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutter_(nautical) "Rutter (nautical)") (mariner's handbook) containing vital information on the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_China_Trade "Old China Trade"), India, and Japan trade routes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-McCulloch-23)

In 1596, three more English ships sailed east but all were lost at sea.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-igi-ii-p454-19) A year later however saw the arrival of [Ralph Fitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Fitch "Ralph Fitch"), an adventurer merchant who, with his companions, had made a remarkable nine year overland journey to [Mesopotamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia "Mesopotamia"), the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf"), the Indian Ocean, India and Southeast Asia.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-25) Fitch was consulted on Indian affairs and gave even more valuable information to Lancaster.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-26)

### Formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Formation")]

In 1599, a group of prominent merchants and explorers met to discuss a potential East Indies venture under a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Anarchy-22):1–2 Besides Fitch[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Anarchy-22):5 the group included [Stephen Soame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Soame "Stephen Soame"), then [Lord Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_London "Lord Mayor of London"); [Thomas Smythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Smythe "Thomas Smythe"), a powerful London politician and administrator; [Richard Hakluyt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hakluyt "Richard Hakluyt"), writer and proponent of [English colonisation of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_colonization_of_the_Americas "British colonization of the Americas"); and several other sea-farers who had served with Drake and Raleigh.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Anarchy-22):1–2

On 22 September, the group stated their intention "to venture in the pretended voyage to the East Indies (the which it may please the Lord to prosper)" and to themselves invest £30,133 (over £4,000,000 in today's money).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-british-history.ac.uk-28) Two days later, the "Adventurers" reconvened and resolved to apply to the Queen for support of the project.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-british-history.ac.uk-28) Although their first attempt had not been completely successful, they sought the Queen's unofficial approval to continue. They bought ships for the venture and increased their investment to £68,373.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

They convened again a year later, on 31 December 1600, and this time they succeeded; the Queen responded favourably to a petition by [George, Earl of Cumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Clifford,_3rd_Earl_of_Cumberland "George Clifford, 3rd Earl of Cumberland") and 218 others,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-29) including [James Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lancaster "James Lancaster"), [Sir John Harte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harte_(mayor) "John Harte (mayor)"), [Sir John Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Spencer_(Lord_Mayor_of_London) "John Spencer (Lord Mayor of London)") (both of whom had been [Lord Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_London "Lord Mayor of London")), the adventurer [Edward Michelborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Michelborne "Edward Michelborne"), the nobleman [William Cavendish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cavendish,_1st_Earl_of_Devonshire "William Cavendish, 1st Earl of Devonshire") and other [aldermen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldermen "Aldermen") and citizens.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-EIC-Charters-30) She granted her charter to their corporation named **Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies**.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-igi-ii-p454-19) For a period of fifteen years, the charter awarded the company a monopoly[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-31) on English trade with all countries east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the [Straits of Magellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Magellan "Straits of Magellan").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-32) Any traders there without a licence from the company were liable to forfeiture of their ships and cargo (half of which would go to the Crown and half to the company), as well as imprisonment at the "royal pleasure".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-33)

The charter named [Thomas Smythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Smythe "Thomas Smythe") as the first governor[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-EIC-Charters-30):3 of the company, and 24 [directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_East_India_Company_directors "British East India Company directors") (including James Lancaster)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-EIC-Charters-30):4 or "committees", who made up a Court of Directors. They, in turn, reported to a Court of Proprietors, who appointed them. Ten committees reported to the Court of Directors. By tradition, business was initially transacted at the Nags Head Inn, opposite [St Botolph's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Botolph-without-Bishopsgate "St Botolph-without-Bishopsgate") church in [Bishopsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishopsgate "Bishopsgate"), before moving to East India House on [Leadenhall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadenhall_Street "Leadenhall Street").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-34)

[James Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lancaster "James Lancaster") commanded the first East India Company voyage in 1601.

[Sir James Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_James_Lancaster "Sir James Lancaster") commanded the first East India Company voyage in 1601 aboard [_Red Dragon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Dragon_(ship) "Red Dragon (ship)").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-35) The following year, whilst sailing in the [Malacca Straits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malacca_Strait "Malacca Strait"), Lancaster took the rich 1,200 ton Portuguese carrack _Sao Thome_ carrying pepper and spices. The booty enabled the voyagers to set up two "[factories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_(trading_post) "Factory (trading post)")" (trading posts) – one at [Bantam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantam_(city) "Bantam (city)") on [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java") and another in the [Moluccas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molucca "Molucca") (Spice Islands) before leaving.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dulles106-36) On return to England in 1603, they learned of Elizabeth's death, but Lancaster was knighted by the new king, [James I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I"), on account of the voyage's success.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-37) By this time, the [war with Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Spanish_War_(1585%E2%80%931604) "Anglo-Spanish War (1585–1604)") had ended but the company had profitably breached the Spanish-Portuguese duopoly; new horizons opened for the English.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Wernham-20)

In March 1604, Sir [Henry Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Middleton_(captain) "Henry Middleton (captain)") commanded the company's [second voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_voyage_to_Asia "Second voyage to Asia"). General [William Keeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Keeling "William Keeling"), a captain during the second voyage, led the third voyage aboard _Red Dragon_ from 1607 to 1610 along with _Hector_ under Captain [William Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_William_Hawkins "Sir William Hawkins") and _Consent_ under Captain [David Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Middleton_(mariner) "David Middleton (mariner)").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-East_India_Company_1897_vi-38)

Early in 1608, [Alexander Sharpeigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Sharpeigh "Alexander Sharpeigh") was made captain of the company's _Ascension_, and general or commander of the fourth voyage. Thereafter, two ships, _Ascension_ and _Union_ (captained by Richard Rowles), sailed from Woolwich on 14 March 1608.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-East_India_Company_1897_vi-38) This expedition was lost.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Mill1817-39)

Initially, the company struggled in the [spice trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice_trade "Spice trade") because of competition from the [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company"). This rivalry led to military skirmishes, with each company establishing fortified trading posts, fleets, and alliances with local rulers. The Dutch, better financed and supported by their government, gained the upper hand by establishing a stronghold in the spice islands (now [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia")), enforcing a near-monopoly through aggressive policies that eventually drove the EIC to seek trade opportunities in India instead. The English company opened a [factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_(trading_post) "Factory (trading post)") (trading post) in [Bantam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banten_(town) "Banten (town)") on Java on its first voyage, and imports of [pepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_pepper "Black pepper") from Java remained an important part of the company's trade for twenty years.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-40)

[_Red Dragon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Dragon_(ship) "Red Dragon (ship)") fought the Portuguese at the [Battle of Swally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Swally "Battle of Swally") in 1612, and made several voyages to the [East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Indies "East Indies").

The emperor [Jahangir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahangir "Jahangir") investing a courtier with a robe of honour, watched by [Sir Thomas Roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Thomas_Roe "Sir Thomas Roe"), English ambassador to the court of Jahangir at Agra from 1615 to 1618, and others

English traders frequently fought their Dutch and Portuguese counterparts in the Indian Ocean. The company achieved a major victory over the Portuguese in the [Battle of Swally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Swally "Battle of Swally") in 1612, at [Suvali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suvali "Suvali") in [Surat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surat "Surat"). The company decided to explore the feasibility of a foothold in mainland India, with official sanction from both Britain and the [Mughal Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire"), and requested that the Crown launch a diplomatic mission.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-fordham1-41)

#### Foothold in India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Foothold in India")]

See also: [Establishment of English trade in Bengal (1610–1900)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Kolkata#Establishment_of_English_trade_in_Bengal_(1610%E2%80%931900) "History of Kolkata")

Company ships docked at [Surat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surat "Surat") in [Gujarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarat_under_Mughal_Empire "Gujarat under Mughal Empire") in 1608.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Tracy-42) The company's first Indian factory was established in 1611 at [Masulipatnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machilipatnam "Machilipatnam") on the [Andhra Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_Andhra "Coastal Andhra") of the [Bay of Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal "Bay of Bengal"), and its second in 1615 at Surat.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-43)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Tracy-42) The high profits reported by the company after landing in India initially prompted James I to grant subsidiary licences to other trading companies in England. However, in 1609, he renewed the East India Company's charter for an indefinite period, with the proviso that its privileges would be annulled if trade was unprofitable for three consecutive years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1615, James I instructed Sir [Thomas Roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Roe "Thomas Roe") to visit the Mughal Emperor Nur-ud-din Salim [Jahangir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahangir "Jahangir") (r.1605–1627) to arrange for a commercial treaty that would give the company exclusive rights to reside and establish factories in Surat and other areas. In return, the company offered to provide the Emperor with goods and rarities from the European market. This mission was highly successful, and Jahangir sent a letter to James through Sir Thomas Roe:[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-fordham1-41)

> Upon which assurance of your royal love I have given my general command to all the kingdoms and ports of my dominions to receive all the merchants of the English nation as the subjects of my friend; that in what place soever they choose to live, they may have free liberty without any restraint; and at what port soever they shall arrive, that neither Portugal nor any other shall dare to molest their quiet; and in what city soever they shall have residence, I have commanded all my governors and captains to give them freedom answerable to their own desires; to sell, buy, and to transport into their country at their pleasure. For confirmation of our love and friendship, I desire your Majesty to command your merchants to bring in their ships of all sorts of rarities and rich goods fit for my palace; and that you be pleased to send me your royal letters by every opportunity, that I may rejoice in your health and prosperous affairs; that our friendship may be interchanged and eternal.

—Nuruddin Salim Jahangir, Letter to James I.

#### Expansion in present-day South Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Expansion in present-day South Asia")]

See also: [List of Anglo-Indian wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Anglo-Indian_wars "List of Anglo-Indian wars")

The company, which benefited from imperial patronage, soon expanded its commercial trading operations. It eclipsed the Portuguese [Estado da Índia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_da_%C3%8Dndia "Estado da Índia"), which had established bases in [Goa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goa "Goa"), [Chittagong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong "Chittagong"), and [Bombay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay "Bombay"); Portugal later ceded Bombay to England as part of the [dowry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowry "Dowry") of [Catherine of Braganza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Braganza "Catherine of Braganza") on her marriage to King [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"). The East India Company also launched a joint attack with the Dutch [United East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_East_India_Company "United East India Company") (VOC) on Portuguese and Spanish ships off the coast of China that helped secure EIC ports in China,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-44) independently attacking the Portuguese in the [Persian Gulf Residencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf_Residency "Persian Gulf Residency") primarily for political reasons.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-45) The company established [trading posts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post") in [Surat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surat "Surat") (1619) and [Madras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chennai "Chennai") (1639).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Cadell1956-46) By 1647, the company had 23 factories and settlements in India, and 90 employees.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-47) Many of the major factories became some of the most populated and commercially influential cities in Bengal, including the walled forts of [Fort William](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_William,_India "Fort William, India") in Bengal, [Fort St George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_St_George "Fort St George") in Madras, and [Bombay Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Castle "Bombay Castle").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The first century of the Company, despite its original profits coming primarily from piracy in the [Spice Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maluku_Islands "Maluku Islands") between competing European powers and their companies,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48) saw the East India Company change focus after suffering a major setback in 1623 when their factory in [Amboyna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amboyna_massacre "Amboyna massacre") in the Moluccas was attacked by the Dutch. This compelled the company to formally abandon their efforts in the Spice Islands, and turn their attention to Bengal where, by this time, they were making steady, if less exciting, profits.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48) After gaining the indifferent patronage of the [Mughal Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire"), whose cities were "the megacities of their time" and whose wealth was unrivalled outside of Asia in the 17th century,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48) the Company's first century in the Mughal-ruled areas was spent cultivating their relationship with the [Mughal Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_dynasty "Mughal dynasty"), and conducting peaceful trade at great profit. At first, it should be said the EIC was drawn into the Mughal system, acting as a kind of vassal to Mughal authority in present-day Bangladesh: it was from this position that the Company would ultimately outplay and outmanoeuvre all competing powers in the region, to eventually use that very system to hold power itself.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48)

What started as trading posts on undesirable land were developed into sprawling factory complexes with hundreds of workers sending exotic goods to England and managing protected points to export English finished goods to local merchants. The Company's initial rise in Bengal and successes generally came at the expense of competing European powers through the art of currying favours and well-placed bribes, as the Company was matched at every step by French expansion in the region (whose [equivalent company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV's_East_India_Company "Louis XIV's East India Company") carried substantial royal support). Throughout the entire century, the company only resorted to force against the Mughals once, with terrible consequences.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48) The [Anglo-Mughal war (1686–1690)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Mughal_war_(1686%E2%80%931690) "Anglo-Mughal war (1686–1690)") was a complete defeat, ending when the EIC effectively swore fealty to the Mughals to get their factories back. The East India Company's fortunes changed for the better in 1707 when Bengal and other regions under Mughal rule fell into anarchy after the death of the Mughal Emperor [Aurangzeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb "Aurangzeb").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48) A series of large-scale rebellions, and the collapse of the Mughal taxation system led to the effective independence of virtually all of the pre-1707 Mughal fiefs and holdings, with their capital Delhi routinely under the control of Maratha, Afghan, or usurper generals' armies. The EIC was able to take advantage of this chaos, slowly assuming direct control of the province of [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal "Bengal"), and fighting [numerous wars against the French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnatic_wars "Carnatic wars") for control of the east coast of the subcontinent. The Company's position in the Mughal court as it fell apart made it possible to sponsor various powerful people on the subcontinent as they individually contended with others, steadily amassing more land and power in India to themselves.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the 18th Century, the primary source of the Company's profits in Bengal became taxation in conquered and controlled provinces, as the factories became fortresses and administrative hubs for networks of tax collectors that expanded into enormous cities. The Mughal Empire was the richest in the world in 1700, and the East India Company tried to strip it bare for a century thereafter. Dalrymple calls it "the single largest transfer of wealth until the Nazis".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48) What was in the 17th century the production capital of the world for textiles was forced to become a market for British-made textiles. Statues, jewels, and various other valuables were moved from the palaces of Bengal to the townhouses of the English countryside. Bengal in particular suffered the worst of Company tax farming, highlighted by the [Great Bengal famine of 1770](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Bengal_famine_of_1770 "Great Bengal famine of 1770").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48)

The Company found its first real territorial and financial foothold in India via the Battle of Plassey.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:1-49) The battle took place on June 23, 1757, wherein [Robert Clive’](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Clive "Robert Clive")s force of roughly 800 soldiers and 2,200 sepoys defeated the [Nawab of Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawabs_of_Bengal "Nawabs of Bengal"), [Siraj ud-Daula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siraj-ud-Daulah "Siraj-ud-Daulah").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:2-50) The company was victorious largely through a prior conspiracy with the Nawab’s commander, [Mir Jafar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_Jafar "Mir Jafar"), instead of through force.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:2-50) The victory installed Mir Jafar as the Nawab and secured the Company a settlement worth £3 million.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:2-50)

Mir Jafar's subsequent dependence on Company backing drew the Company steadily deeper into the government of Bengal, culminating in 1765 when the Mughal emperor [Shah Alam II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Alam_II "Shah Alam II") granted it the diwani, the right to collect and administer the revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. This gave the Company a public revenue on a scale previously unmatched by any other European trading enterprise, and allowed it to pay for its exports of Bengali cloth and other goods out of local tax revenue rather than by shipping bullion from Britain, a pattern historians such as Robins have called "unrequited trade." In effect, the Company had become a territorial and fiscal power as much as a commercial one.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:1-49)

The primary tool of expansion for the company was the Sepoy. The [Sepoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepoy "Sepoy") were locally raised with European training and equipment, who changed warfare in present-day South Asia. Mounted forces and their superior mobility had been king on the region's battlefields for a thousand years, with cannon so well integrated that the Mughals fought with cannon mounted on elephants; all were no match for line infantry with decent discipline supported with field cannon. Repeatedly, a few thousand company sepoys fought vastly larger Mughal forces numerically and came out victorious. Afghan, Mughal, and Maratha factions started creating their own European-style forces, often with French equipment, as the chaos intensified and the stakes were raised. Ultimately, the company won out, generally through as much diplomacy and statecraft as through fraud and deception. The gradual rise of the East India Company within the Mughal network culminated in the [Second Anglo-Maratha War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Maratha_War "Second Anglo-Maratha War"), in which the Company successfully ousted the Maratha, the Empire's official protectors, at the high water point in their rise to power, and installed a young Mughal Prince as Emperor, with the Company as the de jure protectors of the Empire from their position of direct control in Bengal. This relationship was repeatedly strained as the Company continued its expansion and exploitation; however, it lasted in some form until 1858, when the last Mughal Emperor was exiled as the Company was disbanded and its assets were taken over by the British Crown.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Dalrymple2019-48)

In 1634, the Mughal emperor [Shah Jahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Jahan "Shah Jahan") extended his hospitality to English traders to [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal "Bengal"), the richest region of the empire,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-51) and in 1717 customs duties were completely waived for the English in Bengal. By then, the Company's mainstay businesses were in cotton, silk, opium, [indigo dye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo_dye "Indigo dye"), [saltpetre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate "Potassium nitrate") and tea. Meanwhile, the Dutch, the Company's most aggressive competitors, had expanded their monopoly of the spice trade in the [Straits of Malacca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Malacca "Straits of Malacca") by ousting the Portuguese in 1640–1641. With reduced Portuguese and Spanish influence in the region, the EIC and VOC entered a period of intense competition, resulting in the [Anglo-Dutch wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Dutch_wars "Anglo-Dutch wars") of the 17th and 18th centuries. The British were also interested in trans-Himalayan trade routes, as they would create access to untapped markets for British manufactured goods in Tibet and China.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-52) This economic interest was showcased by the [Anglo-Nepalese war (1814–1816).](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Nepalese_war "Anglo-Nepalese war")

#### Expansion throughout Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Expansion throughout Asia")]

Within the first two decades of the 17th century, the Dutch East India Company or _Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie_ (VOC) was the wealthiest commercial operation in the world with 50,000 employees worldwide and a private fleet of 200 ships. It specialised in the spice trade and gave its shareholders a 40% annual dividend.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-53)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The British East India Company was fiercely competitive with the Dutch and French throughout the 17th and 18th centuries over spices from the [Spice Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice_Islands "Spice Islands"). Some spices, at the time, could only be found on these islands, such as nutmeg and cloves; and they could bring profits as high as 400 per cent from one voyage.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Suijk2015-54) The tension was so high between the Dutch and the British East Indies Trading Companies that it escalated into at least four Anglo-Dutch wars:[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Suijk2015-54) 1652–1654, 1665–1667, 1672–1674 and 1780–1784. Competition arose in 1635 when Charles I granted a trading licence to Sir [William Courteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Courten "William Courten"), which permitted the rival [Courteen association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courteen_association "Courteen association") to trade with the East at any location in which the EIC had no presence.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-55) In an act aimed at strengthening the power of the EIC, King Charles II granted the EIC (in a series of five acts around 1670) the rights to autonomous territorial acquisitions, to mint money, to command fortresses and troops and form alliances, to make war and peace, and to exercise both civil and criminal jurisdiction over the acquired areas.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-56)

In 1689, a Mughal fleet commanded by [Sidi Yaqub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidi_Yaqub "Sidi Yaqub") attacked Bombay. After a year of resistance, the EIC surrendered in 1690, and the company sent envoys to [Aurangzeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb "Aurangzeb")'s camp to plead for a pardon. The company's envoys had to prostrate themselves before the emperor, pay a large indemnity, and promise better behaviour in the future. The emperor withdrew his troops, and the company subsequently re-established itself in Bombay and set up a new base in Calcutta.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-encyclopedia.com-57)

#### Slavery 1621–1834

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Slavery 1621–1834")]

The East India Company's archives suggest its involvement in the slave trade began in 1684, when a Captain Robert Knox was ordered to buy and transport 250 slaves from [Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar") to [St. Helena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Helena "St. Helena").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-59) The East India Company began using and transporting slaves in Asia and the Atlantic in the early 1620s, according to the [Encyclopædia Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-topic/East-1) or in 1621, according to Richard Allen.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-60) Eventually, the company ended the trade in 1834 after numerous legal threats from the British state and the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") in the form of the [West Africa Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Squadron "West Africa Squadron"), which discovered various ships had contained evidence of the illegal trade.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-61)

#### Japan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Japan")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Bodleian_Library_MS._Jap._b.2_Shuinjo.jpg/250px-Bodleian_Library_MS._Jap._b.2_Shuinjo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_MS._Jap._b.2_Shuinjo.jpg)

A document with the original [vermilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermilion "Vermilion") seal of [Tokugawa Ieyasu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_Ieyasu "Tokugawa Ieyasu"), granting trade privileges in Japan to the East India Company in 1613

In 1613, during the rule of [Tokugawa Hidetada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_Hidetada "Tokugawa Hidetada") of the [Tokugawa shogunate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_shogunate "Tokugawa shogunate"), the British ship [_Clove_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clove_(ship) "Clove (ship)"), under the command of Captain [John Saris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Saris "John Saris"), was the first English ship to call on Japan. Saris was the chief factor of the EIC's trading post in Java, and with the assistance of [William Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Adams_(sailor,_born_1564) "William Adams (sailor, born 1564)"), an English sailor who had arrived in Japan in 1600, he was able to gain permission from the ruler to establish a commercial house in [Hirado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirado,_Nagasaki "Hirado, Nagasaki") on the Japanese island of [Kyushu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyushu "Kyushu"):

> We give free license to the subjects of the King of Great Britaine, Sir Thomas Smythe, Governor and Company of the East Indian Merchants and Adventurers forever safely come into any of our ports of our Empire of Japan with their shippes and merchandise, without any hindrance to them or their goods, and to abide, buy, sell and barter according to their own manner with all nations, to tarry here as long as they think good, and to depart at their pleasure.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-62)

Unable to obtain Japanese [raw silk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raw_silk "Raw silk") for export to China, and with their trading area reduced to Hirado and [Nagasaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagasaki "Nagasaki") from 1616 onwards, the company closed its factory in 1623.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-63)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Anglo-Mughal War")]

Main article: [Anglo-Mughal war (1686–1690)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Mughal_war_(1686%E2%80%931690) "Anglo-Mughal war (1686–1690)")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/The_English_ask_pardon_of_Aurangzeb.jpg/250px-The_English_ask_pardon_of_Aurangzeb.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_English_ask_pardon_of_Aurangzeb.jpg)

[French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") illustration of [Sir Josiah Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah_Child "Josiah Child") requesting a pardon from the [Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Emperor "Mughal Emperor")[Aurangzeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb "Aurangzeb")

The first of the [Anglo-Indian wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Indian_wars "Anglo-Indian wars") occurred in 1686 when the company conducted naval operations against [Shaista Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaista_Khan "Shaista Khan"), the governor of [Mughal Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Bengal "Mughal Bengal"). This led to the siege of Bombay and the subsequent intervention of the Mughal Emperor, [Aurangzeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb "Aurangzeb"). Subsequently, the English company was defeated and fined.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-65)

**Mughal convoy piracy incident of 1695**

Main article: [Ganj-i-Sawai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganj-i-Sawai "Ganj-i-Sawai")

In September 1695, Captain [Henry Every](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Every "Henry Every"), an English pirate on board the [_Fancy_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fancy_(pirate_ship) "Fancy (pirate ship)"), reached the Straits of [Bab-el-Mandeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab-el-Mandeb "Bab-el-Mandeb"),[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] where he teamed up with five other pirate captains to attack the Indian fleet returning from the annual pilgrimage to [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca "Mecca"). The Mughal convoy included the treasure-laden _[Ganj-i-Sawai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganj-i-Sawai "Ganj-i-Sawai")_, reported to be the greatest in the Mughal fleet and the largest ship operational in the Indian Ocean, and its escort, the _Fateh Muhammed_. They were spotted passing the straits en route to [Surat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surat "Surat"). The pirates gave chase and caught up with the _Fateh Muhammed_ some days later, and meeting little resistance, took some £40,000 of silver.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Burgess_2009-66):136–137

Every continued in pursuit and managed to overhaul _Ganj-i-Sawai_, which resisted strongly before eventually [striking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Striking_the_colours "Striking the colours"). _Ganj-i-Sawai_ carried enormous wealth and, according to contemporary East India Company sources, was carrying a relative of the [Grand Mughal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangazeb "Aurangazeb"), though there is no evidence to suggest that it was his daughter and her retinue. The loot from the _Ganj-i-Sawai_ had a total value between £325,000 and £600,000, including 500,000 gold and silver pieces, and has become known as the richest ship ever taken by pirates.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-67)

When the news arrived in England, it caused an outcry. To appease Aurangzeb, the East India Company promised to pay all financial reparations, while [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") declared the pirates _[hostis humani generis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hostis\_humani\_generis "Hostis humani generis")_ ("the enemy of humanity").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-68)[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In mid-1696 the government issued a £500 bounty on Every's head and offered a free pardon to any informer who disclosed his whereabouts. The first worldwide manhunt in recorded history was underway.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Burgess_2009-66):144

The plunder of Aurangzeb's treasure ship had serious consequences for the English East India Company. The furious Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb ordered Sidi Yaqub and [Nawab Daud Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawab_Daud_Khan "Nawab Daud Khan") to attack and close four of the company's factories in India and imprison their officers, who were almost lynched by a mob of angry [Mughals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_(tribe) "Mughal (tribe)"), blaming them for their countryman's depredations, and threatened to put an end to all English trading in India. To appease Emperor Aurangzeb and particularly his [Grand Vizier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Vizier "Grand Vizier")[Asad Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asad_Khan_(Mughal_noble) "Asad Khan (Mughal noble)"), Parliament exempted Every from all of the [Acts of Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_grace_(piracy) "Acts of grace (piracy)") (pardons) and amnesties it would subsequently issue to other pirates.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-69)[_[disputed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Disputed statement")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:East\_India\_Company#Henry\_Avery\_and\_Acts\_of\_Grace "Talk:East India Company")_]

#### China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: China")]

The British began trading with China in 1699.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-70) This fact is recorded from the Chinese side in _[The Draft History of the Qing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qingshi\_gao "Qingshi gao")_ under the year Kangxi 37 (1698).[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-71) The apparent discrepancy between the British and Chinese sources can be explained by the fact that [Chinese New Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_New_Year "Chinese New Year") of 1699 did not fall until 31 January, so that any treaties entered into in January would have been logged under Kangxi 37 rather than Kangxi 38. In 1715 the Company established a permanent "[factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_(trading_post) "Factory (trading post)")" in [Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou") (Canton).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-72)

The company started selling opium to Chinese merchants in the 1770s in exchange for goods like [porcelain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain "Porcelain") and tea,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-73) causing a series of [opioid addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opioid_use_disorder "Opioid use disorder") outbreaks across China in 1820.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-74) The ruling [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") outlawed the opium trade in 1796 and 1800,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-75) but British merchants continued illegally nonetheless.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-76)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-77) The Qing took measures to prevent the East India Company from selling opium, and destroyed tens of thousands of chests of opium already in the country.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-78) This series of events led to the [First Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War "First Opium War") in 1839, which involved a succession of British naval attacks along the Chinese coast over the course of several months. As part of the [Treaty of Nanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Nanking "Treaty of Nanking") in 1842, the Qing were forced to give British merchants special treatment and the right to sell opium. The Chinese also ceded territory to the British, including the island of [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Island "Hong Kong Island").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-79)

Within India, opium was grown for export by peasant farmers in the north in what are now Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, under a monopoly run through an Opium Agency of clerks who enforced contracts and quality standards.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:3-80) According to the economic historian Rolf Bauer farmers received less for their raw opium than it cost to grow and the system relied on advance payments, production targets and coercion.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:3-80)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-81) The Company's opium trade was exploitative and left millions of Indian farmers impoverished.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-:3-80)

### Forming a monopoly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Forming a monopoly")]

#### Trade monopoly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Trade monopoly")]

The prosperity that the officers of the company enjoyed allowed them to return to Britain and establish sprawling estates and businesses, and to obtain political power, such as seats in the House of Commons.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Guha2016-82) Ship captains sold their appointments to successors for up to £500. As recruits aimed to return to Britain wealthy by securing Indian money, their loyalties to their homeland increased.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Guha2016-82)

The company developed a [lobby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying "Lobbying") in the English parliament. Pressure from ambitious tradesmen and former company associates (pejoratively termed _Interlopers_ by the company), who wanted to establish private trading firms in India, led to the passing of the deregulating act in 1694.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-victorianweb.org-83)

This act allowed any English firm to trade with India, unless specifically prohibited by an Act of Parliament, thereby annulling the charter that had been in force for almost 100 years. When the **East India Company Act 1697** ([9 Will. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9_Will._3 "9 Will. 3"). c. 44) was passed in 1697, a new "parallel" East India Company (officially titled the _English Company Trading to the East Indies_) was floated under a state-backed indemnity of £2 million.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-Boggart-87) The powerful stockholders of the old company quickly subscribed a sum of £315,000 in the new concern, and dominated the new body. The two companies wrestled with each other for some time, both in England and in India, for a dominant share of the trade.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-victorianweb.org-83)

It quickly became evident that, in practice, the original company faced scarcely any measurable competition. The companies merged in 1708, by a tripartite indenture involving both companies and the state, with the charter and agreement for the new **United Company of Merchants of England Trading to the East Indies** being awarded by [Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Godolphin,_1st_Earl_of_Godolphin "Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-88) Under this arrangement, the merged company lent a sum of £3,200,000 to the Treasury, in return for exclusive privileges for the next three years, after which the situation was to be reviewed.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-victorianweb.org-83)

A constant battle between the company lobby and Parliament followed for decades. The company sought a permanent establishment, while Parliament would not willingly allow it greater autonomy and so relinquish the opportunity to exploit the company's profits. In 1712, the **East India Company Act 1711** was passed, which renewed the status of the company, though the debts were repaid. By 1720, 15% of British imports were from India, almost all passing through the company, which reasserted the influence of the company lobby. The licence was prolonged until 1766 by yet another act in 1730.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-89)

At this time, Britain and France became bitter rivals. Frequent skirmishes between them took place for control of colonial possessions. In 1742, fearing the monetary consequences of a war, the British government agreed to extend the deadline for the licensed exclusive trade by the company in India until 1783, in return for a further loan of £1 million. Between 1756 and 1763, the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War") diverted the state's attention towards consolidation and [defence of its territorial possessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") in Europe and its [colonies in North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_colonisation_of_the_Americas "English colonisation of the Americas").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-oxforddnb.com-90)

The war partly took place in the Indian theatre, between the company troops and the French forces. In 1757, the [Law Officers of the Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Officers_of_the_Crown "Law Officers of the Crown") delivered the [Pratt–Yorke opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt%E2%80%93Yorke_opinion "Pratt–Yorke opinion") distinguishing overseas territories acquired by [right of conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_conquest "Right of conquest") from those acquired by private treaty. The opinion asserted that, while the Crown of Great Britain enjoyed sovereignty over both, only the property of the former was vested in the Crown.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-oxforddnb.com-90) With the advent of the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), Britain surged ahead of its European rivals. Demand for Indian commodities was boosted by the need to sustain troops and the economy during the war, and by the increased availability of raw materials and efficient methods of production. As home to the revolution, Britain experienced higher standards of living. Its ever-growing cycle of prosperity, demand and production had a profound influence on overseas trade. The company became the single largest player in the British global market. In 1801 [Henry Dundas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Dundas,_1st_Viscount_Melville "Henry Dundas, 1st Viscount Melville") reported to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") that

> ... on the 1st March, 1801, the debts of the East India Company amounted to 5,393,989 _[l.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound\_sterling "Pound sterling")_ their effects to 15,404,736 _l._ and that their sales had increased since February 1793, from 4,988,300 _l._ to 7,602,041 _l._[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-91)

#### Saltpetre trade

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=East_India_Company&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Saltpetre trade")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Potassium_nitrate.jpg/250px-Potassium_nitrate.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Potassium_nitrate.jpg)

[Saltpetre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate "Potassium nitrate") used for [gunpowder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder "Gunpowder") was one of the major trade goods of the company.

Sir [John Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_John_Banks,_1st_Baronet "Sir John Banks, 1st Baronet"), a businessman from [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent") who negotiated an agreement between the king and the company, began his career in a syndicate arranging contracts for [victualling the navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victualling_Commissioners "Victualling Commissioners"), an interest he kept up for most of his life. He knew that [Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys") and [John Evelyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evelyn "John Evelyn") had amassed a substantial fortune from the [Levant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant") and Indian trades. He became a director and later, as governor of the East India Company in 1672, he arranged a contract which included a loan of £20,000 and £30,000 worth of [saltpetre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate "Potassium nitrate")—also known as potassium nitrate, a primary ingredient in [gunpowder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpowder "Gunpowder")—for the King "at the price it shall [sell by the candle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candle_auction "Candle auction")"—that is by auction—where bidding could continue as long as an inch-long candle remained alight.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-92)

Outstanding debts were also agreed, and the company was permitted to export 250 tons of saltpetre. Again in 1673, Banks successfully negotiated another contract for 700 tons of saltpetre at £37,000 between the king and the company. So high was the demand from armed forces that the authorities sometimes turned a blind eye to the untaxed sales. One governor of the company was even reported as saying in 1864 that he would rather have the saltpetre made than the tax on salt.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company#cite_note-93)
